ch01.note: The War of Resistance against Japan (1937–45), the Chinese name for the war set off by the Marco Polo Bridge Incident; from the Nationalist standpoint the central struggle of the age. Chen dates the events of his book by it.

Chen's central term is tewu gongzuo (特务工作), the covert operations of the Nationalist secret service: intelligence, sabotage, turning enemy agents, and targeted killing. The word tewu (secret agent) carries an unsavoury ring in Chinese, and his defence of the work is the theme of the third introduction.
The Chinese is huokou (活口), literally 'a living mouth': the one witness left alive to tell what happened, a phrase with an underworld chill.
Those who died for the state were honoured by having their tablets enshrined in a Martyrs' Shrine (忠烈祠) and by posthumous commendation.
The book's title, Yingxiong wuming (英雄无名), reads literally 'heroes, nameless': the men of the secret service who died unknown, their names in no history.

Chen projected the memoir in five books. Four were completed and are collected here; the fifth, on his own arrest and imprisonment in Shanghai, was never finished. This is the 'five-part plan' referred to later.

ch02.note: Dai Li (戴笠, 1897–1946), courtesy name Yunong (雨农), founder and lifelong head of the Nationalist secret service. A Whampoa man, he built the service from the early 1930s until his death in a 1946 air crash; feared and powerful, he is the presiding figure of Chen's story.

Chen gives dates by the Republican calendar, which counts from the founding of the Republic in 1912, so that Republican year n is 1911 + n (thus year 21 is 1932). Such dates are converted to the Western year throughout this translation.
Beiping ('Northern Peace') was the name of Beijing from 1928, when the Nationalists made Nanjing their capital, until 1949; it is called Beiping throughout the book.
The Kang-Ri Shajian Tuan (抗日杀奸团), a group of patriotic young people in occupied North China who assassinated collaborators.
An irregular anti-Japanese force in the Luan River and Shanhaiguan area of eastern Hebei (滦榆游击队).
A Station (站, zhan) was the service's local field office; Chen headed those at Beiping and Tianjin. A larger regional command was a District (区), such as the Shanghai District he later ran.
Zhang Jingyao (张敬尧, 1881–1933), a Beiyang-era general and former military governor of Hunan; assassinated in the Beiping Legation Quarter in 1933 for conspiring with the Japanese.
The Beiyang (北洋) clique, the military strongmen who dominated China between Yuan Shikai's death in 1916 and the Nationalist reunification of 1928.
The walled diplomatic quarter of Beiping, east of Tiananmen, where the foreign legations held extraterritorial rights and Chinese police could not enter.
Sun Chuanfang (孙传芳, 1885–1935), a major Beiyang warlord styled commander-in-chief of five provinces; broken by the Northern Expedition and later assassinated.
Shi Jianqiao (施剑翘) shot Sun Chuanfang dead in a Tianjin Buddhist hall in 1935 to avenge her father, whom Sun had executed; the celebrated case ended in a public pardon.

Ji Hongchang (吉鸿昌, 1895–1934), a former Northwest Army general who joined the 1933 Chahar anti-Japanese army; executed by the Nationalists in 1934. In the People's Republic he is honoured as a Communist martyr, the reverse of the account Chen gives here.
Feng Yuxiang (冯玉祥, 1882–1948), the 'Christian General,' a powerful and frequently-shifting warlord and a founder of the 1933 Chahar anti-Japanese army.
A former province of the North China and Inner Mongolian borderland, north-west of Beiping; abolished in 1952.

Chen writes in the Nationalist idiom, ascribing Ji Hongchang's revolt to Communist direction. Historians treat the Chahar anti-Japanese army as a broad united-front venture; Ji did join the Communist Party in 1932, but the flat attribution here is the memoir's partisan reading, not settled fact.
Shi Yousan (石友三, 1891–1940), a general notorious for switching allegiances again and again; killed by his own side in 1940.
Yin Rugeng (殷汝耕, 1885–1947), head of the Japanese-sponsored 'East Hebei Anti-Communist Autonomous Government' (1935–38); tried and executed as a traitor after the war.
Wang Kemin (王克敏, 1879–1945), head of the Japanese puppet 'Provisional Government of the Republic of China' at Beiping; nicknamed 'Blind Wang' for his failing sight.
Bushido (武士道), 'the way of the warrior,' the Japanese samurai code of honour and willingness to die.

ch02.anchor: anyone may put them to death
ch02.note: A classical maxim in the Confucian tradition: rebellious ministers and unfilial sons are fair game for any hand. Chen invokes it to justify the killings as righteous.

ch03.note: A provisional English rendering of Chen's title for Book Two, Henei ru ming (河内辱命), roughly 'orders dishonoured at Hanoi.' He set that title aside; the book was published as The Full Story of the Wang Case at Hanoi (河内汪案始末), and he discusses his choice of titles in its Author's Preface.

Wang Jingwei (汪精卫, 1883–1944), a founding Nationalist leader and rival of Chiang Kai-shek who broke with Chongqing in December 1938 to seek peace with Japan and, from 1940, headed a Japanese-sponsored government at Nanjing. The 1939 attempt on his life at Hanoi is the subject of Book Two.
Then the capital of Tonkin in French Indochina, where Wang Jingwei took refuge after leaving Chongqing; foreign soil beyond Chinese jurisdiction.
Wang's so-called yan telegram (艳电, the yandian) of December 1938, which publicly urged a negotiated peace with Japan: his open break with the resistance.
A shuanghuang (双簧), a comic turn in which one performer mouths the words another speaks from behind: here the suspicion that Wang's 'defection' was staged in secret collusion with Chongqing.
Chongqing (重庆), in Sichuan, was the wartime capital of Nationalist China from 1938; the seat of the government committed to resistance.
Chen Bijun (陈璧君, 1891–1959), Wang Jingwei's wife and a forceful political figure in her own right; imprisoned after the war.

ch03.anchor: opening of the government at Nanjing
ch03.note: Wang Jingwei's Reorganized National Government, inaugurated at Nanjing in March 1940 under Japanese sponsorship, in rivalry with Chongqing.
The Hanoi action team. Chen names several of them here (Yu Jiansheng, Wang Luqiao, Tang Yingjie), whose parts fill the narrative of Book Two.

ch04.note: A District (区, qu) was a regional command of the service, larger than a Station; Chen was chief of the Shanghai District from 1939.

Throughout, 'the Juntong' renders 军统 / 军统局, short for the Bureau of Investigation and Statistics of the Military Affairs Commission (军事委员会调查统计局), the Nationalists' military secret service under Dai Li. The full name dates strictly from 1938; Chen uses it loosely for the whole lineage that began with the Lixingshe's Special Services Department in 1932 (see the Prefatory Note), so its use for the earlier years is a mild anachronism.
'Sanction' renders 制裁 (zhicai), the service's own euphemism for the targeted killing or execution of a traitor or enemy; the term is kept throughout.
Fu Xiao'an (傅筱庵, 1872–1940), a banker installed as puppet mayor of Shanghai; assassinated in his bed in 1940 by his own cook, an agent of the resistance.
Zhang Xiaolin (张啸林), one of the 'Three Tycoons' of the Shanghai Green Gang, alongside Du Yuesheng and Huang Jinrong; killed in 1940 for collaborating with the Japanese.
Li Shiqun (李士群, 1905–1943), a former Communist who ran the Wang regime's secret police at No. 76 Jessfield Road in Shanghai; poisoned by the Japanese in 1943.
The Wang regime's dreaded secret-police apparatus (特工总部), known from its address as 'No. 76.'
The Kempeitai (宪兵队), the Japanese army's military police, which ran counter-intelligence and repression in occupied China.
The Tokko (特高), the 'special higher police,' the Japanese political-police branch.
The Ume Kikan (梅机关, 'Plum Blossom Agency'), the Japanese special-service organ that engineered Wang Jingwei's defection and his Nanjing regime.
A former Tokkō officer of the Japanese military police at Nanjing whom Chen met again in Taipei in 1980. The Japanese reading of his name is reconstructed from the Chinese characters (大冢清).
From the Mencius: the mark of the 'great man' is that riches and honour cannot corrupt him, poverty and low estate cannot swerve him, power and force cannot bend him.
The radical clique led by Mao Zedong's wife Jiang Qing, blamed for the worst of the Cultural Revolution; arrested in 1976, a month after Mao's death.

Liu Shaoqi (刘少奇, 1898–1969), head of state of the People's Republic, purged and hounded to death during the Cultural Revolution; Tao Zhu (陶铸) was another senior victim. Chen notes with irony that the Communists branded their own fallen leaders 'Kuomintang secret agents.'

The Kaohsiung (Formosa) Incident of December 1979, a pro-democracy demonstration in Taiwan broken up by the Nationalist authorities and followed by mass trials. Chen, a career security man, writes of the dissidents with hostility.

Mao Zedong (毛泽东), leader of the Chinese Communist Party. Chen refers to him elsewhere as Mao qiu (毛酋), 'the Mao chieftain' or 'bandit chief Mao'; the Nationalist idiom that casts the Communist leadership as bandits is preserved throughout.
Lin Biao (林彪) and Nie Rongzhen (聂荣臻), the Communist commanders whose armies encircled and took Beiping and Tianjin in the winter of 1948–49.

'Pacification' (绥靖) and, later, 'suppression of the rebellion' (戡乱) are the Nationalist terms for the 1946–49 civil war, casting the Communists as rebels to be put down. They are kept as Chen's own idiom.

Zheng Jiemin (郑介民) and Mao Renfeng (毛人凤) headed the postwar secret service after Dai Li's death. The Bureau of Confidential Investigation (保密局, the Baomiju) was the Juntong's renamed successor from 1946.
The treaties imposed on China from the 1840s that granted foreign powers concessions and extraterritorial rights on Chinese soil: the legal reason Chinese police could not act inside the Concessions.
The foreign-run Shanghai International Settlement and the adjacent French Concession, self-governing enclaves outside Chinese jurisdiction.

An allusion to Zhang Liang's failed ambush of the First Emperor of Qin at Bolang, whose iron missile struck the wrong carriage: hence, killing the wrong man. It also titles a later chapter of the book.
Zeng Zhongming (曾仲鸣, 1896–1939), Wang Jingwei's close aide, killed at Hanoi in the attack meant for Wang.
From a Tang anecdote of a would-be hermit who won office by a show of reclusion on Mount Zhongnan; the phrase means a back-door route to a career.

ch05.note: The Mukden Incident of 18 September 1931, in which the Japanese army seized Manchuria: the opening of Japan's aggression against China.
The Shanghai Incident of 28 January 1932, a month of fighting between Japanese and Chinese forces around Shanghai.
The Nationalist officer academy near Guangzhou (founded 1924), whose graduates formed the core of Chiang Kai-shek's army and of the secret service; a 'Whampoa man' was one of this favoured clique.

ch05.anchor: the Three Principles of the People
ch05.note: Sun Yat-sen's political doctrine of Nationalism, Democracy, and the People's Livelihood (三民主义), the founding ideology of the Kuomintang.
The 'Society for Vigorous Practice of the Three Principles of the People' (三民主义力行社), a secret organization of Whampoa officers formed in 1932 and popularly known as the 'Blue Shirts.'
The covert-operations department (特务处) of the Lixingshe, directed by Dai Li: the operational seed from which the Juntong grew.
The bureau (调查统计局) set up under the Military Affairs Commission in 1932; its Second Department, under Dai Li, was the government-side face of the same secret-service work and grew into the Juntong.
A second-tier body (革命军人同志会) under the Lixingshe, one tier of the layered organization through which the secret service operated.

ch06.note: 'The Commandant' (校长) is Chiang Kai-shek, who as head of the Whampoa Military Academy and its Nanjing successor was addressed by his officers and cadets as 校长 for the rest of his life. Chen uses it, together with 'the Leader' (领袖) and 'the Generalissimo' (委员长, chairman of the Military Affairs Commission), throughout as reverent names for Chiang; 蒋公 is the honorific 'Mr. Chiang.'

The 中山装 (Zhongshan zhuang), the high-collared four-pocket tunic named for Sun Yat-sen (Sun Zhongshan) and known in the West as the 'Mao suit' from its later Communist use; in this period it was the plain everyday dress of Nationalist officials and officers.

ch06.anchor: Central Military Academy Special Research Class
ch06.note: The 中央军校 (Central Military Academy) was the Nanjing successor, from 1928, to the Whampoa Military Academy; its graduates are the 'academy classmates' who fill this book. The 'Special Research Class' was a small, hand-picked study group under its political department.

ch06.anchor: several books the Commandant himself had prescribed
ch06.note: The prescribed works are Neo-Confucian and statecraft classics: the collected works of Lu Xiangshan (Lu Jiuyuan, 1139-1193) and of Wang Yangming (1472-1529), the two great idealist philosophers of the mind; the collected works of Zeng Guofan (posthumous title Wenzheng, 1811-1872), the Qing statesman and general who suppressed the Taiping rebellion; and the military maxims of Qi Jiguang (1528-1588), the Ming general famed for defeating the coastal pirates. The last title is a modern exposition of Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People.
So called because the building's plan had the shape of the character 工 (gong) - an I-shape of two long halls joined by a shorter passage between.
中正 (Zhongzheng) is Chiang Kai-shek's formal given name, with which he signed official documents; the familiar 'Chiang Kai-shek' is the Cantonese reading of another of his names, 介石 (Jieshi).

The Whampoa Academy and its successor numbered their graduating classes (期, qi): the first class graduated in 1924, and seniority ran strictly by class, so that a man of an earlier class was an 'elder brother' (老大哥) to those of later ones. Chen was of the fifth class, Dai Li nominally of the sixth.
The yuan (元) was the silver dollar, the standard currency of Republican China; forty to eighty yuan was a modest but livable monthly stipend for a junior officer at this time.

Hu Hanmin (1879-1936), a leading Kuomintang theorist and rival of Chiang Kai-shek; Chiang's detention of him in 1931 touched off a revolt of the southern Guangdong-Guangxi leaders, whose anti-Chiang movement the book here calls a 'New Kuomintang.'
From the proverb 上有天堂，下有苏杭, 'Above there is Heaven; below, there are Suzhou and Hangzhou' - the two lower-Yangtze cities long held the fairest and most prosperous places on earth.
洪公祠, a shrine hall to a 'Lord Hong,' which gave its name to the training ground behind it; in Juntong lore the 'Honggongci Training Class' became the legendary cradle of the service's field officers.
The Cheka (切卡, from the Russian ChK) was the Soviet political police founded in 1917, forerunner of the OGPU, NKVD, and KGB, and a byword for the modern secret service.

Four brotherhoods of the Chinese underworld and secret-society world: the Sandianhui ('Three Dots Society,' a Triad branch) and the Gelaohui ('Elder Brothers Society') of the Yangtze provinces, and the Green Gang (青帮) and Red or Hong Gang (洪帮) - the last the great sworn-brotherhood networks of Republican Shanghai.

ch06.anchor: the eyes and ears of the Leader
ch06.note: 领袖耳目、兄弟手足 - a couplet Dai Li later composed as the motto of his service: its members were to be the eyes and ears of the Leader (Chiang) and hands and feet to one another.

The 中统 (Central Statistics Bureau of the Kuomintang's Organization Department) was the party's civilian secret service, grown from this Investigation Section and run by the Chen brothers' 'CC Clique'; it was the lifelong rival of Dai Li's military 'Juntong.'
阁子, Beiping dialect for the neighborhood police box or substation; literally a 'little pavilion.'
The Chinese Youth Party (中国青年党), founded 1923, a small nationalist and anti-Communist third party opposed alike to the Kuomintang and the Communists.
六国饭店, the 'Six Nations Hotel,' known in French as the Grand Hôtel des Wagons-Lits, a leading foreign hotel in the Legation Quarter of Beiping; it was there that Zhang Jingyao was shot.

On 4 June 1928 the Japanese Kwantung Army blew up the train of the Manchurian warlord Zhang Zuolin (the 'Old Marshal') at Huanggutun near Mukden, killing him; the deed opened the way to Japan's later seizure of the Northeast.
四公子, 'the Four Young Masters' - a loose epithet, varying in the telling, for the famous playboy sons of prominent Republican political and military families.

四维学会; the 四维 are the 'Four Cardinal Bonds' named by the ancient statesman Guan Zhong - 礼义廉耻, propriety, righteousness, integrity, and a sense of shame - which the Nationalists made a watchword of their New Life Movement.

In December 1936 Zhang Xueliang and Yang Hucheng seized Chiang Kai-shek at Xi'an and held him until he agreed to a united front with the Communists against Japan; Zhang was thereafter placed under a house arrest that lasted more than fifty years.

Itagaki Seishirō (1885-1948; the standard reading of 板垣, here written 坂垣), a general of the Japanese Kwantung Army and an architect of the 1931 seizure of Manchuria; later war minister, he was hanged as a war criminal in 1948.

The Baoding Military Academy (保定军官学校, 1912-1923), the principal training school for Chinese army officers before Whampoa; many senior commanders of the warlord and Nationalist armies were its graduates.

ch07.note: Rehe (热河), or Jehol, a former province of the mountainous borderland north-east of Beiping. In February–March 1933 the Japanese Kwantung Army overran it in a swift campaign (the “Operation Nekka”), annexing it to the puppet state of Manchukuo and carrying the fighting down to the passes of the Great Wall; the province was abolished in 1955.

Cai E (蔡锷, 1882–1916), the Yunnan general who in 1915 slipped out of Yuan Shikai’s Beijing—by popular legend with the help of the sing-song girl Xiao Fengxian (小凤仙), whose favours gave him his cover—to raise the National Protection War against Yuan’s attempt to make himself emperor. Their romance became a stock subject of opera, stage, and screen, which is the “Xiao Fengxian” Chen means.

The 八大胡同, a cluster of lanes just south of Qianmen that formed Beiping’s licensed pleasure quarter. The first-class houses advertised themselves as “pure-singing houses” (清吟小班), where in principle the women sold their song and their company rather than their bodies; 平康里 (Pingkangli) is a classical literary name for such a district.

打茶围, the custom of a paid introductory visit to a courtesan: the guest sits with her over tea, melon seeds, cigarettes, and talk, appraising her while she appraises his purse. It carried a set fee and, at a proper “home” room, formally opened the acquaintance; it implied nothing further of itself.
Zhang Zongchang (张宗昌, 1881–1932), warlord of Shandong, nicknamed the “Dog-Meat General,” a byword for brute cruelty, uncounted concubines, and buffoonery; driven out in 1928 and assassinated in 1932.

Manchukuo (满洲国), the puppet state Japan set up in the Northeast in 1932 under the last Qing emperor, Puyi. The Japanese aim Chen describes was to engineer a comparable client regime across North China—the project the Zhang Jingyao affair was part of.

ch07.anchor: The Secret Records of President Chiang
ch07.note: 蒋总统秘录, a documentary biography of Chiang Kai-shek drawn largely from Nationalist archives, serialized in Japan’s Sankei Shimbun in the mid-1970s and issued in Chinese translation by the Central Daily News (中央日报) in Taipei. Chen quotes the Chinese edition.

Duan Qirui (段祺瑞, 1865–1936), the Beiyang premier and head of the Anhui clique who dominated the Beijing government in the late 1910s; by 1933 long out of power and living in retirement, which is why the Japanese hoped to draw him out.

Song Zheyuan (宋哲元, 1885–1940), commander of the Twenty-Ninth Army in North China; his troops fought the Japanese at the Great Wall passes in 1933 and again at the Marco Polo Bridge in July 1937. Zhang Jingyao’s claim of “deep ties” to him, on which Itagaki paid out, appears to have been a boast.

ch07.anchor: A Tale of Heroic Sons and Daughters
ch07.note: 儿女英雄传, a mid-nineteenth-century novel by Wen Kang. Its heroine, Shisanmei (十三妹, “Thirteenth Sister”) He Yufeng, sets out to avenge her murdered father but is dissuaded before she can strike—hence Chen’s point that Shi Jianqiao, who did carry her revenge through, went a step further.

The Xinchou Treaty (辛丑条约) of 1901, imposed on the Qing by the eight allied powers after the Boxer Uprising. It fixed a vast indemnity and formalized the Legation Quarter as a walled, foreign-garrisoned enclave into which Chinese authority could not reach—the “humiliating brand” Chen names.

ch08.note: The Tanggu Truce (塘沽协定), signed 31 May 1933, ended the fighting that followed the Japanese seizure of Rehe and the Kwantung Army’s push to the Great Wall. It fixed a demilitarized zone across eastern Hebei from which Chinese forces were barred, leaving the approaches to Beiping and Tianjin under effective Japanese control. The Nationalist government presented it as a necessary breathing-space; its critics called it a surrender of sovereignty—the very charge Chen describes disaffected figures such as Feng Yuxiang seizing upon.

ch08.anchor: a pair of old men of the Green Gang
ch08.note: The Green Gang (青帮) was a sworn brotherhood and secret society, rooted among the boatmen of the Grand Canal and grown by the Republican era into a powerful criminal and political fraternity, strongest in the Yangtze cities. Members were ranked by fixed “generation” characters (here the “Tong” rank), and a senior man initiated new disciples in a formal ceremony called “opening the incense hall” (开香堂)—which is why a gathering of men with no women present was mistaken for a conspiratorial meeting.

The Peking Union Medical College (北平协和医学院), founded in 1906 and re-endowed from 1915 by the Rockefeller Foundation, was the most prestigious modern medical school in China; its degree marked an elite Western-trained physician.

The Mackenzie Memorial Hospital (马大夫纪念医院) in the British concession at Tianjin, named for the Scottish medical missionary John Kenneth Mackenzie; his surname, transliterated, gave the colloquial Chinese name “Dr. Ma” (马大夫).

ch08.anchor: The Lishunde Hotel is the first name in Tianjin
ch08.note: The Lishunde (利顺德大饭店), known in English as the Astor House Hotel, opened in the British concession in 1863 and was the oldest and grandest Western-style hotel in Tianjin, a byword for luxury and expense.

ch08.anchor: though I did not kill Boren
ch08.note: An allusion to the Book of Jin. The statesman Wang Dao, believing his friend Zhou Yi (styled Boren) had failed to defend him, let Zhou go to his execution unopposed; only afterward did he find the memorials in which Zhou had secretly pleaded for his life, and cried, “Though I did not kill Boren, Boren died because of me.” The phrase names a death one did not intend but must in conscience answer for.

The “Mauser” (驳壳枪) is the German C96 semi-automatic pistol, distinguished by its boxy fixed magazine and a detachable wooden holster that clips on as a shoulder-stock—hence the northern nicknames “box” (盒子) and “wood-shell” (木壳). Cheap, hard-hitting, and imported or copied in vast numbers, it was the signature sidearm of warlord China, of its bandits, and of its secret agents.

The “Blue Shirt Society” (蓝衣社) was the name by which outsiders—the press, the Japanese, and above all the Communists—knew the secret Nationalist fraternity that Chen calls the Lixingshe and the Renaissance Society. The label (from a supposed uniform) fastened on the organization a lurid reputation as Chiang Kai-shek’s fascist-style terror apparatus. Chen, writing from within, treats “Blue Shirts” as an enemy’s coinage; that Ji Hongchang should imagine himself dueling with it is, to him, a Communist fantasy.
The pun is on “red” (红): both the building’s red brick and the “red” Communist cause it secretly served.

ch08.anchor: I grieve I did not die resisting Japan
ch08.note: This five-word quatrain, said to have been written by Ji Hongchang on the execution ground, is honored in the People’s Republic as his martyr’s testament and is inscribed at his memorials. Chen, as an interested witness on the opposing side, doubts its authenticity and takes it for a posthumous Communist embellishment.

ch08.anchor: a great riot of "Red Guards" broke out at Zhengzhou
ch08.note: During the Cultural Revolution (1966–76) the “Red Guards” (红卫兵) were militant student factions first mobilized by Mao Zedong; by 1967–68 rival factions, some armed and backed by army units, fought pitched battles across China. Chen’s contemptuous “Mao hag” renders 毛婆, a jeer at Jiang Qing, Mao’s wife and a leader of the radical faction; Lin Biao was then Mao’s defense minister and designated successor.

The Dagongbao (大公报, “L’Impartial”), founded at Tianjin in 1902, was the most respected independent Chinese newspaper of the Republican era. The Shenbao (申报) cited just below was Shanghai’s leading daily.

ch09.anchor: the first taste of defeat the "Beiping Station" had had
ch09.note: A note on the order of this book’s sub-sections. The source divides this section into six numbered parts, one through six; but it prints the part numbered four after the part numbered five (the account of the author’s flight and exile). The transposition is the original’s, whether by the author’s design or a printer’s slip, and it is preserved here rather than silently reordered.

ch09.anchor: Minister He presiding over the military and civil affairs of North China
ch09.note: He Yingqin (何应钦, 1890–1987), a senior Nationalist general and, at this time, Chiang Kai-shek’s chief military deputy in the north as head of the Beiping Branch Military Council. It was he who, in June 1935, signed the He–Umezu Agreement, by which Nationalist forces and Party organs were withdrawn from Hebei under Japanese pressure—the concession that opened the way to the “autonomous” North China of the years this section describes.

The coalition war of 1930, in which Yan Xishan (阎锡山), the militarist governor of Shanxi, and Feng Yuxiang joined the southern opposition against Chiang Kai-shek’s Nanjing government. Known to historians as the Central Plains War (中原大战), it was the largest of the warlord conflicts of the Nanjing decade, drawing in more than a million men before Zhang Xueliang’s intervention on Chiang’s side decided it. Shi Yousan’s repeated changes of allegiance, recounted here, run through this war and its aftermath.

Doihara Kenji (土肥原贤二, 1883–1948), the Kwantung Army intelligence officer who ran Japanese covert operations in North China and Manchuria and was nicknamed in the Western press “the Lawrence of Manchuria.” He engineered the removal of the last Qing emperor Puyi to Manchukuo and, in 1935, the puppet East Hebei regime. He was tried as a Class-A war criminal and hanged in 1948.

ch09.anchor: the k'ang of the western wing-room
ch09.note: The kang (炕), the standard bed of north China: a broad platform of brick or clay built along a wall, with flues beneath it carrying the smoke and heat of the household stove, so that the sleeping-surface stays warm through the bitter northern winter. A family’s daytime life—sitting, eating, working—is also carried on upon it.

In the folk reckoning of north China the depth of winter is counted in “nines” (数九): the eighty-one coldest days are told off in nine periods of nine days each, beginning at the winter solstice, and the cold is deepest in the third and fourth nines. To be out on horseback in “the nine-nines” is to be abroad in the hardest of the year.

ch09.anchor: to go by night to Guisui and seek refuge
ch09.note: Guisui (归绥)—the twin old-and-new town of Guihua and Suiyuan, today Hohhot—was the seat of Suiyuan, a sparsely settled frontier province on the edge of the Mongolian steppe northwest of Beiping. For a man of the metropolitan cities it was true exile: the section’s title, “a flight into frontier exile,” is meant literally.

The Green Gang ranked its members by seniority in a fixed sequence of generation-names, each initiate belonging to the “generation” of the master who brought him in and standing above those of the generations below. “Tong” (通) was one such generation-name; to be of it, and reckoned “the twenty-second,” placed the author at a defined rung in the gang’s hierarchy—a standing, as he says, higher in the northwest than in the gang’s Shanghai heartland.

The Japanese campaign of 1935 to detach the five northern provinces from Nanjing’s control under the guise of local “autonomy.” It yielded the puppet East Hebei Autonomous Council under Yin Rugeng and, as a Chinese counter-move, the semi-independent Hebei–Chahar Political Council under Song Zheyuan—the body, named here as the North China Political Affairs Council, whose thankless dealings with the Japanese garrison form the backdrop to Shi Yousan’s rehabilitation.

ch10.anchor: had likewise "sanctioned" the Prince Regent of the Manchu Qing
ch10.note: In April 1910 the young Wang Jingwei, then a revolutionary, was arrested for a plot to assassinate Zaifeng, Prince Chun, the regent for the child emperor Puyi of the Qing dynasty. Condemned to life imprisonment, he wrote in his cell the celebrated quatrain quoted here (“With a full heart he sang in the market of Yan …”), which made him a hero of the revolution. Chen sets these lines, and the memory of the idealistic young assassin, against the elderly collaborator whose killing this book records—an irony he means his readers to feel.

The “Yan Telegram” (艳电). Chinese telegrams of the day marked their date with a single character standing for the day of the month (a convention called 韵目代日); the character 艳 stood for the twenty-ninth. Wang Jingwei’s open telegram of 29 December 1938, which sued for peace with Japan on the basis of Prime Minister Konoe’s statement, became the public signal of his defection. Its full text is given, and taken apart line by line, in the next chapter.

Konoe Fumimaro (近卫文麿, 1891–1945), Prime Minister of Japan for most of 1937–39 and again in 1940–41. His three public statements of 1938 set out Japan’s terms for ending the war; the third, of 22 December 1938, was the one Wang Jingwei answered.

ch10.anchor: chairman of the People's Political Council
ch10.note: The People’s Political Council (国民参政会), a wartime advisory assembly set up by the National Government in 1938 to represent the parties and public bodies backing the resistance. That Wang Jingwei was its chairman made his defection the more scandalous.

ch11.note: The Juntong kept a shrine, in the manner of a lineage’s ancestral hall (祠堂), where the spirit-tablets of its fallen agents were enshrined and honored—a mark of the service’s image of itself as a brotherhood bound beyond death.

ch11.anchor: the ever more formidable "Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps
ch11.note: The Anti-Japanese Traitor-Killing Corps (抗日杀奸团, abbreviated 抗团), a clandestine band of patriotic young people—many of them students—in Japanese-occupied Beiping and Tianjin, who assassinated collaborators and enemy agents. It worked in concert with Chen’s Juntong organization, and its members suffered heavy losses to the Japanese gendarmerie.

ch11.anchor: the affairs of the "Luan-Yu Guerrilla Command,"
ch11.note: The Luan-Yu Guerrilla Command (滦榆游击总部) took its name from the Luan River (滦河) and Yuguan—Shanhaiguan, the pass where the Great Wall meets the sea—the eastern reach of Hebei bordering the Japanese-held Northeast. It was the Juntong’s guerrilla command in that region, headed by Wang Tianmu.

ch11.anchor: As was mentioned in the fifth section of the first book
ch11.note: Chen refers to a fifth section of Rooting Out Traitors in the North; as collected in this edition that book runs to four numbered sections (here Chapters 6–9). The discrepancy is the original’s—perhaps a slip, or a reference to material differently divided in an earlier printing—and is left as written.

Chen’s name for the cycle-rickshaw, or cyclo, of French Indochina, in which the passenger rides in a seat in front while the driver pedals behind—the reverse of the Chinese rickshaw. The name invokes Zhuge Liang (styled Kongming), the legendary strategist of the Three Kingdoms to whom folklore credits the invention of ingenious carts.

“Director-General” (总裁) was Chiang Kai-shek’s title as head of the Nationalist Party, which he assumed in 1938; it is distinct from his military title of Generalissimo (委员长) and his academy title of Commandant (校长). Wang Jingwei, as Vice-Director-General (副总裁), was the party’s second-ranking figure—which is why the telegram is addressed, pointedly, to Chiang and the party’s committees.

Not to be confused with Sun Yat-sen’s Three Principles of the People. These were the three points of Prime Minister Konoe’s statement of 22 December 1938—good-neighborly amity, joint defense against communism, and economic cooperation—on which Wang Jingwei proposed to make peace.

In November 1938, at the Chongguangtang (重光堂) in Shanghai, Wang Jingwei’s envoys Gao Zongwu and Mei Siping secretly negotiated with the Japanese officers Kagesa Sadaaki and Imai Takeo the terms—the so-called “Chongguangtang agreement”—on which Wang would break with Chongqing. Chen adduces these earlier talks to show that Wang’s claim, in the Yan Telegram, to have “just read” the Konoe statement was a pretense.

ch11.anchor: I have already arranged with him
ch11.note: The source here is garbled: it reads 我已经和他的爱 (“I have already, with his … love”), which yields no sense. The meaning evidently intended is that Dai Li had already settled with the contact that Chen alone would be his liaison; the corrupt phrase is rendered here to that sense.

ch11.anchor: as plainly apart as the Jing and the Wei
ch11.note: A Chinese proverb: the Jing River runs clear and the Wei muddy, and where they meet the two stay distinct (泾渭分明); hence a plain and unmistakable difference—here, between those for war and those for peace.

ch12.note: The eighteen luohan (Sanskrit arhat), the perfected disciples of the Buddha who guard the Dharma—a stock set of eighteen figures in Chinese temple statuary; here a wry nickname for the eighteen-man Hanoi team. “The Eighteen Little Vajra-guardians” (十八小金刚) plays on the same convention, the vajrapala being the fierce, muscular temple guardians.

The battle of Tai’erzhuang (台儿庄), fought March–April 1938 around the walled town of that name in southern Shandong, was the first major Chinese victory of the war and a great lift to morale. Chinese accounts of the day claimed tens of thousands of Japanese killed; the far smaller figures the source itself gives in parentheses—the Japanese-admitted 2,367 dead and 9,615 wounded—point up the gap, and the true scale of Japanese losses remains disputed among historians.

ch12.anchor: Long Yun, the chairman of Yunnan province
ch12.note: Long Yun (龙云, 1884–1962), the Yi (Lolo) military strongman who ruled Yunnan as its provincial chairman from 1927 to 1945, commanding his own provincial army. His near-independence made Kunming a natural way-station on Wang Jingwei’s flight; whether he was privy to the plan beforehand is a question Chen weighs and leaves open.

ch12.anchor: the building of a 'New Order in East Asia'
ch12.note: The “New Order in East Asia” (東亞新秩序, J. Toa shin-chitsujo), proclaimed in Konoe’s statement of 3 November 1938, was Japan’s slogan for a Japanese-led bloc of Japan, “Manchukuo,” and China—dressed as deliverance from Western imperialism but amounting to Japanese mastery of the region. It is the object of Chiang’s rebuttal in this chapter.

The Japanese statements quoted here consistently use 支那 (J. Shina) for China, a name Chinese of the day held contemptuous. It is rendered “Shina” wherever the Japanese texts use it, to keep the flavor of the original, and “China” elsewhere.

The Five Ministers’ Conference (五相會議, J. Gosho kaigi), an inner council of the Japanese cabinet—the premier and the war, navy, foreign, and finance ministers—which in 1938 became the body where the highest China-policy decisions were taken, a mark of the army’s grip on the state.

The Koain (興亞院, “Asia Development Board”), set up in December 1938 as the central organ coordinating Japanese political, economic, and cultural policy in occupied China, largely under military control. The earlier name Chen mentions, the “Tai-Shi Board” (對支院, “Board for China”), used the derogatory 支.

ch12.anchor: the "Twenty-One Demands" he exacted of Yuan Shikai
ch12.note: The Twenty-One Demands (二十一條) that Japan pressed on China in 1915, seeking sweeping economic and political controls; their partial acceptance became a lasting emblem of national humiliation. Yuan Shikai (袁世凱, 1859–1916) was then President of the Republic.

The Nine-Power Treaty, signed at the Washington Conference in 1922 by Japan, the United States, and others, pledged its signatories to respect China’s sovereignty and the “Open Door” of equal commercial opportunity. Japan’s war and its “New Order” were open breaches of it.

ch12.anchor: the Korea of the Treaty of Shimonoseki
ch12.note: By the Treaty of Shimonoseki (馬關條約, 1895) that ended the first Sino-Japanese War, China gave up its suzerainty over Korea, which was declared “independent”; Japan made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it outright in 1910. Chiang’s point is that Japanese-sponsored “independence” was the prelude to annexation.

The Zhanggufeng Incident (張鼓峰事件, known in Russian as the battle of Lake Khasan), a border clash between Japanese and Soviet forces near the Korea–USSR frontier in July–August 1938, in which the Japanese came off the worse. Shigemitsu Mamoru (重光葵, 1887–1957) was then Japan’s ambassador at Moscow.

The “Tanaka Memorial” (田中奏摺) purported to be a secret 1927 memorial from premier Tanaka Giichi to the throne, laying out a program of world conquest beginning with China (“to conquer the world, one must first conquer China”). Widely circulated in China and the West as proof of Japanese designs, it is now generally regarded by historians as a forgery, most likely of Chinese origin, and its authenticity was already doubted when Chiang cited it. The “Meiji legacy-policy” (明治遺策) is the allied notion of a continental expansion bequeathed by the Meiji founders.

ch12.anchor: when Tanaka sent troops to Jinan
ch12.note: In May 1928, as the Nationalists’ Northern Expedition drove toward Beijing, Japanese troops sent by the cabinet of Tanaka Giichi (田中義一, 1864–1929, premier and foreign minister 1927–29) occupied Jinan and clashed bloodily with the Nationalist army—the “Jinan Incident.” Chiang’s point is that the Revolutionary Army pressed on to Beiping regardless.

“The Party Leader” (總理, zongli) is Sun Yat-sen (孫中山, 1866–1925), founder of the Nationalist Party, whose party title of Director-General was retired in his honor after his death; the weekly “Party Leader’s Memorial Week” (總理紀念週) was a standard assembly at which his testament was read. Chiang’s own parallel party title, 總裁, is rendered “Director-General” elsewhere in this book.

ch12.anchor: what Jin Xiongbai wrote under the pen name Zhu Zijia
ch12.note: Jin Xiongbai (金雄白, 1904–1985), a journalist who served in the Wang Jingwei regime and, writing after the war under the pen name Zhu Zijia (朱子家), produced a long insider memoir of it, The Rise and Fall of the Wang Regime (汪政權的開場與收場)—a partisan but much-cited source.

ch12.anchor: Set beside Hirota's Three Principles of former days
ch12.note: The “Three Principles” put to China in 1935 by the government of Hirota Koki (廣田弘毅, 1878–1948), then Japan’s foreign minister and later premier: Chinese suppression of anti-Japanese activity, tacit recognition of “Manchukuo,” and joint defense against communism. China never accepted them; Chiang cites them as milder than Konoe’s later demands.

ch13.anchor: released from Xifeng county in Guizhou
ch13.note: Xifeng, a county in Guizhou province, was the site of the Juntong’s own concentration camp—a secret detention centre where the service held its own suspect members and political prisoners. Chen’s guarded phrase, that it was “the very spot where our own working comrades go to observe the law,” is bitter irony: a man of the secret service could be imprisoned by it as readily as its enemies.

ch13.anchor: No. 27 Gao Lang Street (in transliteration)
ch13.note: Wang Jingwei’s Hanoi residence stood on the street Chen transliterates as Gao Lang Street—the Rue Colombert of the French colonial city (today Cao Ba Quat). Numbers 25–27 were the scene of the assassination attempt of March 1939, the central event toward which these chapters build.

ch13.anchor: the Fourteenth Air Force of the American General Chennault
ch13.note: Claire L. Chennault (1893–1958), the American aviator who organised the volunteer “Flying Tigers” (the American Volunteer Group) to fight the Japanese over China, later absorbed into the United States Fourteenth Air Force under his command.

ch13.anchor: the Prince Regent Zaifeng at Beijing
ch13.note: Zaifeng (1883–1951), Prince Chun, was the father of the boy-emperor Puyi and served as Prince Regent for the last years of the Qing. Wang’s 1910 plot to bomb him, and the celebrated prison verse it produced, made Wang a revolutionary hero—the fame his later collaboration would betray.

ch13.anchor: those four widely-loved quatrains
ch13.note: The best known line of these verses, “the knife brings one glad stroke—I grudge not this young head,” became a byword for youthful revolutionary self-sacrifice and was recited by a generation. After Wang’s defection it was turned against him, quoted in mockery of the hero who had outlived his own courage.

ch13.anchor: and founded the Tongmenghui
ch13.note: The Tongmenghui (“United League” or Revolutionary Alliance), founded by Sun Yat-sen at Tokyo in 1905 by merging several anti-Qing societies, was the direct forerunner of the Nationalist Party (Kuomintang). Its polemical organ, the Min Bao (“People’s Journal”), waged war on the reformists’ Xinmin Congbao.

ch13.anchor: engaging Zhang Taiyan (Binglin) as editor-in-chief
ch13.note: Zhang Binglin (1869–1936), styled Taiyan, was one of the age’s foremost classical philologists and a fierce anti-Manchu revolutionary. His quarrel with Wang over the editorship of the Min Bao, and his eventual founding of the rival Restoration Society, split the revolutionary camp.

ch13.anchor: the Royalist leader Liang Qichao
ch13.note: Liang Qichao (1873–1929), styled Rengong, and his teacher Kang Youwei led the Baohuanghui (“Protect the Emperor Society”), constitutional monarchists who sought reform under the Qing throne and opposed the republican revolutionaries.

ch13.anchor: the farce of the Hongxian enthronement
ch13.note: Yuan Shikai’s attempt to make himself emperor: he proclaimed a new dynasty under the reign-title Hongxian for 1916, but the near-universal revolt it provoked forced him to abandon the throne within weeks, and he died soon after.

ch13.anchor: the Soviet adviser Borodin
ch13.note: Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), the Comintern’s chief political adviser to the Nationalist Party during the Soviet–KMT alliance of 1923–27, wielding great influence at Guangzhou and Wuhan until the break with the Communists.

ch13.anchor: came the Zhongshan Warship Incident
ch13.note: The incident of March 1926 at Guangzhou, by which Chiang Kai-shek curbed Communist and Soviet influence in the Nationalist army and government and consolidated his own command. Chen’s text dates it the twenty-first; it is conventionally dated the twentieth of March.

ch13.anchor: This is the period called the
ch13.note: In 1927 the Nationalists split into two rival governments: Chiang’s at Nanjing (Ning) and the Communist-influenced left’s at Wuhan (Han). The rupture, and its bloody resolution in the purge of the Communists, is the “Ninghan Split.”

ch13.anchor: the Marco Polo Bridge Incident
ch13.note: The clash of the seventh of July 1937 at the Marco Polo (Lugou) Bridge, southwest of Beiping, which opened the full-scale war between China and Japan and marks the true beginning of China’s eight-year resistance.

ch13.anchor: the German ambassador to China, Trautmann
ch13.note: Oskar Trautmann, Germany’s ambassador, conducted a mediation effort between China and Japan in the winter of 1937–38, before Germany threw its lot fully with Japan. His good offices came to nothing as Japanese demands hardened.

ch13.anchor: doing as Liu Yu and Zhang Bangchang had done
ch13.note: Liu Yu and Zhang Bangchang were the two Chinese officials whom the invading Jurchen Jin set up as puppet emperors over parts of Song China in the 1120s and 1130s (the puppet states of “Qi” and “Chu”). They are the classic Chinese archetype of the traitor installed as the conqueror’s figurehead.

ch13.anchor: of the Franco-Prussian War
ch13.note: Léon Gambetta (1838–1882), the French statesman who, after the collapse of 1870, rallied France to go on resisting the Prussians—here Wang’s fond image of himself as the leader who saves a beaten nation by a bold stroke.

ch13.anchor: likened him to the Latter Ruler Li
ch13.note: Li Yu (937–978), last ruler of the Southern Tang, a supreme lyric poet who lost his kingdom and died a captive. To call a man’s verse the “music of a doomed state” and to liken him to “the Latter Ruler Li” is to say his gifts were those of a ruler fit only to lose.

ch13.anchor: the Classic of Mountains and Seas
ch13.note: The Shanhaijing, an ancient Chinese compendium of geography, myth, and monstrous creatures. The Jingwei bird—the drowned daughter of the Fiery Emperor, forever carrying pebbles to fill the sea—is its archetype of hopeless, dogged perseverance; Wang took the name for his own.

ch13.anchor: Japan annexed our vassal state the Ryukyus
ch13.note: Japan absorbed the Ryukyu Kingdom (a tributary of Qing China) in 1879, making it Okinawa Prefecture. Chen cites this, and the First Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95, as the opening moves of Japan’s long design on China.

ch13.anchor: proposed that Japan send planes to bomb Chongqing
ch13.note: This charge—that Wang solicited Japanese bombing of Chinese cities to break the resistance’s will—Chen reports with an explicit hedge (“whether the report was reliable or not”) and on the authority of the wartime press. It is not corroborated by independent scholarship and should be read as an uncorroborated wartime allegation; the text is kept as Chen wrote it.

ch13.anchor: exposed at Hong Kong the whole secret pact
ch13.note: The defection of January 1940: Gao Zongwu and Tao Xisheng, two of Wang’s own peace negotiators, broke with him, fled to Hong Kong, and published the secret draft agreement Wang had reached with Japan, exposing how far its terms sold Chinese sovereignty and gravely damaging his cause.

ch15.anchor: the way toward the Red River bridge
ch15.note: The great cantilever bridge over the Red (Hong) River at Hanoi, opened in 1902 and long known as the Pont Doumer, after Paul Doumer, the governor-general who had it built; today it is the Long Bien Bridge. Carrying road and rail on a single narrow deck, and here under repair so that traffic crossed one lane at a time, it is the bottleneck on which the car chase turns.

The source spells this operative's surname 'Chen' here in Chapter Five, and so does the Biography of Dai Yunong quoted later in the chapter; but in Chapter Three it was written 'Zheng.' He is one and the same man, and one of the three of the team captured at Hanoi. He is rendered 'Chen Bangguo' throughout this translation, following the fuller and semi-official usage; the discrepancy is the source's own.

A hill resort some hours north of Hanoi. Chen calls it Da Le; the Biography of Dai Yunong quoted below calls the same place Dan Dao, and the Wang-regime memoir calls it San Tao Shan. The three names are not reconciled in the sources, and the exact identification of the resort is uncertain.

ch15.anchor: The Secret Records of President Chiang
ch15.note: Jiang zongtong milu: a large semi-official life of Chiang Kai-shek serialized by the Sankei Shimbun of Japan and compiled from materials supplied by the Nationalist Party History Committee. It is a real work; its account of the Hanoi killing, quoted here, agrees in the main with Chen's own, including the detail that Wang had changed rooms that night.

ch15.anchor: The Biography of Mr. Dai Yunong
ch15.note: Dai Yunong xiansheng zhuan: the 1979 life of Dai Li published by the Intelligence Bureau of the Ministry of National Defense in Taiwan, a real and semi-official work drawn from the service's own archives. Chen treats its account as carrying the weight of an official record, while noting where it differs from his memory.

ch15.anchor: The Rise and Fall of the Wang Regime
ch15.note: Wang zhengquan de kaichang yu shouchang: a history of the Wang Jingwei government by the journalist Jin Xiongbai, writing under the pen name Zhu Zijia. A real work, serialized from 1959 in the Hong Kong magazine Chunqiu and later issued in six volumes; it gives the fullest account from the Wang side, which Chen here quotes and corrects.

ch15.anchor: An Account of the Conduct of Mr. Zeng Zhongming
ch15.note: A xingzhuang is a traditional account of the conduct and career of a person newly dead, drawn up to supply the materials for a formal biography or epitaph. Wang Jingwei composed one for Zeng Zhongming, the aide killed in his place at Hanoi; Zeng, gravely wounded, is said to have died after signing over the funds held in his name and losing too much blood.

Ju yi ge li: a long public statement Wang Jingwei issued on 9 April 1939 defending his call for peace with Japan, in which he cited the record of a wartime meeting of the Supreme National Defense Council. Chen and his contemporaries charged that Wang had tampered with that record; the piece is a real document of the propaganda war that followed the Hanoi attempt.

Wu Jingheng (1865-1953), better known by his courtesy name Zhihui, a revered elder of the Nationalist Party, classical scholar and calligrapher, and one of its senior moral authorities; he had earlier drafted the resolution expelling Wang from the Party. His rejoinder to 'To Cite One Instance' was among the most cutting of the replies to Wang.

ch15.anchor: the new Hiranuma cabinet in Japan
ch15.note: The cabinet of Baron Hiranuma Kiichiro, Japanese prime minister from January to August 1939, which succeeded Konoe's. Its comparative coolness toward Wang left him, for a time, stranded and uncertain of Japanese backing.

ch15.anchor: the guilt reaches not to wife and child
ch15.note: An old principle of Chinese law and morals, that punishment for a crime should not reach a man's wife and children. Chen invokes it to spare the household; the bitter irony is that the raid killed Zeng Zhongming and wounded his wife and several of Wang's people, while Wang himself went unharmed.

ch16.anchor: never one so base as Wang
ch16.note: The chapter title, “Vile Treachery, Illusions Undone,” takes its first half from this diary entry: on 11 April 1939 Chiang Kai-shek wrote of Wang the words rendered here, with the terms ‘false and treacherous’ (奪伪) and ‘base’ (卑劣). The second half of the source title is textually corrupt—a garbled phrase the digital source does not resolve—and is rendered by sense as ‘illusions undone,’ Wang’s scheme collapsing to nothing.

An allusion to Yue Fei (1103–1142), the Song general recalled from a winning campaign against the Jin by twelve successive gold tablets bearing the emperor’s summons, and soon afterward put to death on the contrivance of the chancellor Qin Hui. Wu Jingheng’s point: to let a beaten enemy rest and recover would be a betrayal as bitter as Yue Fei’s recall.

ch16.anchor: true to the boy I was
ch16.note: The closing couplet of a famous poem Wang Jingwei wrote in prison in 1910, awaiting execution for the plot against the Manchu Prince Regent Zaifeng: ‘Gladly I meet the blade, / and keep faith with the young man’s head.’ The lines made Wang a romantic hero of the revolution; Wu Jingheng, and Chinese opinion generally, threw them back at him in reproach once he turned to collaboration.

The Munich Agreement of September 1938, by which Britain’s Neville Chamberlain and France pressed Czechoslovakia to hand Germany the German-speaking Sudetenland; within months Germany occupied the rest, and in March 1939—the month before this essay—Emil Hácha signed the remnant away and stayed on as puppet ‘State President.’ Munich and Hácha are Wu Jingheng’s running analogy for what Wang’s peace would do to China.

ch16.anchor: like Liang Hong and Meng Guang
ch16.note: Liang Hong and his wife Meng Guang, of the Later Han, were the proverbial devoted couple—she is said to have raised the dinner-tray respectfully to the level of her eyebrows—and the phrase stands for a model married pair. Wu Jingheng applies it, with heavy irony, to Wang Jingwei and his wife Chen Bijun.

A pun on the shared final syllable ‘-wei’ in the names of the two men—Konoe (in Chinese, Jinwei) of Japan and Wang Jingwei of China—whom Wu Jingheng casts as partners; he develops it just below into the ‘Duet of the Two Weis,’ a joint Sino-Japanese stage turn.

Jiawu and gengzi are the sexagenary-cycle names of two disasters Wang invokes: the Sino-Japanese War of 1894–95 (jiawu), ended by the humiliating Treaty of Shimonoseki, and the Boxer catastrophe of 1900 (gengzi), ended by the punitive Boxer Protocol of 1901. Both forced crushing terms on China.

Wu Jingheng’s parting ‘one instance’ turned back on Wang: in 1935, as acting president of the Executive Yuan, Wang Jingwei yielded to a Japanese demand and removed General Song Zheyuan as chairman of Chahar province—handing the province, Wu charges, to Japan without a shot, just as Hácha had lately handed over Czechoslovakia.

ch17.note: Zhizhou (志舟) was the courtesy name of Long Yun, the governor of Yunnan; Wang's letter that follows is addressed to him under that personal style. In the Chinese convention a letter opens with the recipient's name and an honorific of respectful address (here 勋鉴, roughly 'for your honored inspection').

No. 76 Jessfield Road became the most notorious address in wartime Shanghai: the headquarters of the Wang regime's secret service under Ding Mocun and Li Shiqun, a byword for the torture and killing of Nationalist and Communist agents. 'No. 76' (七十六号) is still shorthand in Chinese for that organization.

'Changbanpo' (长坂坡, 'Changban Slope') is a celebrated Peking-opera piece drawn from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms, in which the general Zhao Yun fights his way single-handed through Cao Cao's host to rescue his lord's infant son. To bawl a few lines of it, drunk, is to vent bravado and defiance.

The Du residence was the home of Du Yuesheng (1888-1951), boss of Shanghai's Green Gang and a power in the city's underworld and politics, with long-standing ties to the Nationalists and to Dai Li's secret service. Route Doumer lay in the French Concession, the Green Gang's home ground.

The Blue Sky, White Sun, and a Wholly Red Earth flag (青天白日满地红旗) is the national flag of the Republic of China. Because the Wang regime claimed to be the legitimate Nationalist government, it too flew this flag; to tell puppet troops from Chongqing's, the Japanese had Wang add a yellow streamer reading 'Peace, Anti-Communism, National Reconstruction,' as related below.

'Baimei' (百梅) is obscure in the source and is left here in romanization; in context it appears to stand for the secret Shanghai talks of November 1938 between Wang's envoys (Gao Zongwu and Mei Siping) and the Japanese side, at which the terms of Wang's defection were drafted. The character 梅 ('mei,' plum) recurs in the cover-name of Kagesa's agency, the Ume Kikan.

ch17.anchor: Complete Works of Mr. Dai Yunong
ch17.note: The Complete Works of Mr. Dai Yunong (戴雨农先生全集), published in Taipei in 1979, is a Nationalist commemorative compilation honoring Dai Li; like the Biography of Dai Yunong that Chen cites elsewhere, it is an admiring source, and its account is to be weighed with that in mind.

ch17.anchor: True Record of Three Perils on the Shanghai Shore
ch17.note: The 'True Record of Three Perils on the Shanghai Shore' (沪滨三次历险实录) is a memoir by Zheng Xiuyuan, the Shanghai District secretary, recounting narrow escapes in the underground war against the Japanese and the Wang regime; Chen quotes it here for the particulars of Wang Luqiao's arrest.

ch17.anchor: the flood-tide at the mouth of the Qiantang River
ch17.note: The Qiantang bore, near Hangzhou, is the most famous tidal bore in China: around the middle of the eighth lunar month a wall of water surges upriver against the current with a thunderous roar, and has drawn sightseers for centuries. Chen likens to it the approaching drone of the bombers.

ch18.anchor: Deng Yanda, leader of the Third Party
ch18.note: Deng Yanda (邓演达, 1895-1931) was a left-Nationalist military and political leader who broke with Chiang Kai-shek and founded the 'Third Party,' the Provisional Action Committee of the Chinese Kuomintang. He was arrested in Shanghai in 1931 and secretly executed on Chiang's order. Chen's point is the ill omen of a house that had already brought one guest to arrest and death.

ch18.anchor: Ceremony of the Return of the Capital
ch18.note: The 'return of the capital' (还都) was the ceremony of 30 March 1940 at which Wang Jingwei's collaborationist regime proclaimed the 'return' of the National Government to Nanjing, presenting itself as the legitimate successor to the government Chiang Kai-shek had removed to Chongqing. The claim of continuity, symbolized by reusing the Nationalist name and flag, is what Chen derides as 'passing off fish-eyes for pearls.'

Jing Ke (荆轉) and Nie Zheng (聶政) were the most celebrated assassin-retainers of the Warring States period, both given lives in Sima Qian's 'Biographies of the Assassins' (刺客列传). Jing Ke's failed attempt on the King of Qin in 227 BC and Nie Zheng's killing of a rival minister became bywords for the man who gives his life to requite a patron; the sigh 'where are they now?' asks whether such men are still to be found.

Yuhuatai (雨花台), the 'Terrace of Raining Flowers,' is a low hill just south of the Nanjing city wall; long a scenic and Buddhist site, it served through the Republican years as an execution ground, and it was here that the Wang regime shot Dai Jingyuan and Wu Gengshu.

The funeral inscription (烈并常山, roughly 'a valor to rank with Changshan') alludes to Yan Gaoqing (颜棒卿), the Tang official who held Changshan against the rebel An Lushan in 756 and, once taken and reviled, cursed his captor until he was put to death. His loyalty was enshrined by Wen Tianxiang in the 'Song of Righteousness' (the line on 'the tongue of Yan of Changshan'), and 'Changshan' became a standing figure for a martyr's unbending fidelity.

Zhuanji Wenxue (传记文学, 'Biographical Literature'), the Taipei monthly founded in 1962 by Liu Shaotang, long the leading venue for Republican-era memoirs and first-hand historical accounts. It is the journal in which Chen's Nameless Heroes was serialized, and through which the reader letters he cites in this chapter reached him.

ch20.anchor: soul-summoning register in the Hall of the King of Hell
ch20.note: In Chinese Buddhist and folk belief the King of Hell (阎王, Yanwang; fuller 阎罗王, Yama) is the judge of the underworld, and the “soul-summoning register” (勾魂簿) is the ledger by which his infernal runners mark down the doomed and call them below. The image is grim and exact: the accountant’s vouchers, being impossible to destroy, would—once in enemy hands—name the District’s people one by one for death as surely as that register of the dead.

ch20.anchor: one sheet of the Xin Shen Bao
ch20.note: Two Shanghai newspapers of the occupation years. The Xin Shen Bao (新申报) and the Zhonghua Ribao (中华日报) were both published in occupied Shanghai under Japanese and puppet control; the Zhonghua Ribao in particular had been founded in 1932 as the organ of Wang Jingwei’s clique and served his regime. It was in their pages that the enemy printed a full-page account of the case against the captured Shanghai District—the very sheets Chen’s old comrade preserved and here contributes to the book.

ch21.note: The Loyal and Patriotic Army (忠义救国军, Zhōngyì Jiùguójūn) was a guerrilla and irregular force raised from 1938 by Dai Li’s secret service in the Shanghai–Jiangsu–Zhejiang region. Nominally a resistance army, it doubled as a behind-the-lines arm of the Juntong; its Shanghai office, as here, partly served as cover for District work.

ch21.anchor: soon to be joined in marriage
ch21.note: The original phrase, jié wéi Qín-Jìn (结为秦晋), invokes the intermarriages between the ruling houses of the states of Qin and Jin in the Spring and Autumn period; “a match of Qin and Jin” has been the set expression for a marriage alliance between two families ever since.

The Shanghai foreign authorities, above all the International Settlement, built and policed roads beyond their treaty limits into the surrounding Chinese districts. These “extra-settlement roads” (越界筑路, yuèjiè zhùlù) lay in a legal gray zone of disputed jurisdiction, which by 1939 let the Japanese and their puppets operate along them more freely than inside the concessions proper.

A tingzijian (亭子间, literally “pavilion room”) is the small, cheap room over the kitchen and off the stair landing of a Shanghai lane house, a fixture of the city’s cramped middle-class housing and, in the 1930s, proverbially the lodging of struggling writers and clerks.

Bǎixiàngrén (白相人) is Shanghai dialect for an idler or man-about-town, commonly a petty tough who lived by his wits on the edge of the underworld. The white shirt and glossy black trousers Zheng notes were the type’s recognized get-up.

The fabi (法币, “legal tender”) was the paper currency the Nationalist government made China’s sole legal money in 1935. Wartime issue drove it into steep inflation, so a courier’s thirty-eight yuan a month, meagre to begin with, bought steadily less; Chen sets the figure down to mark how poor his people were kept.

Tang Shengzhi (唐生智, 1889–1970), a Hunanese general who rose under the Nationalists and more than once rebelled against Chiang Kai-shek; the rising meant here is one of his anti-Chiang revolts around 1929–30. He later commanded the doomed defense of Nanjing in 1937.

Deng Yanda (邓演达, 1895–1931), a leading left-wing Nationalist, was seized by Chiang Kai-shek’s agents and secretly executed in 1931; the “Deng Yanda affair” refers to that operation. The “Two Guangs affair” (两广事件) was the June 1936 revolt of the Guangdong and Guangxi militarists against Nanjing. Chen means that Wu Naixian had a hand in the secret-service side of both.

ch22.note: In Shanghai’s underworld and property market, large sums were reckoned in “bars” (条子) — small gold ingots. That ten gold bars should be paid merely to secure a telephone number (40000) marks how the Concession economy ran on bullion rather than on the depreciating paper fabi; the same “bars” are the currency of the “key money” Chen pays for his flat below.

The GPU (from the Russian for “State Political Directorate”) was the Soviet secret police of the 1920s, successor to the Cheka and forerunner of the OGPU and NKVD. Chen uses it as a byword for rigorous, ruthless clandestine training; both a suspect colleague here and, later, the traitor Fu Shenglan are said to have passed through it.

ch22.anchor: the famous newspaperman who had been killed years before
ch22.note: Shao Piaowei (邵飘萍, 1886–1926), founder of the Beijing Jingbao and a celebrated crusading journalist, was seized and shot by the warlord Zhang Zuolin’s forces in 1926 — a landmark in the martyrology of the modern Chinese press. Chen flags the coincidence because the Second Action Team’s inner-duty man of the same name was an entirely different person.

An allusion to the Han general Huo Qubing (140–117 BC), who, when the emperor offered him a mansion, is said to have answered: “The Xiongnu are not yet destroyed — why should I make a home?” The Xiongnu were the steppe confederation that menaced Han China; the phrase became the classic vow to set duty to the state before hearth and family. Here it justifies the Juntong’s wartime ban on marriage.

An allusion to the Book of Documents (wei shan jiu ren, gong kui yi kui): “in raising a mound nine ren high, the work may be spoiled for one basketful of earth.” The saying warns that a great labor all but finished can be ruined by a last small failure of resolve; Dai Li invokes it to shame Chen out of accepting an outsider’s money.

Wan Molin (万墨林, 1893–1980), a cousin and the chief business manager of the Green Gang boss Du Yuesheng, and a figure of the Shanghai underworld in his own right. His memoir Bygone Days in Shanghai (沪上往事) is a much-cited insider account of wartime Shanghai; Chen quotes and disputes it here on the collaborator Yu Yefeng.

The “Badlands” (歹土; the source prints 歹士) was the popular name for the western district of Shanghai lying along the “roads built beyond the boundary” — a legal no-man’s-land outside both the Settlement and Chinese jurisdiction. Under Japanese protection it filled with casinos, opium dens, and the gunmen of the puppet No. 76, and became the deadliest ground of the Shanghai terror war of 1939–41.
